explanations: That's what it looks like it should say, and exactly the trap. `bool()` doesn't read the words.
Right. Any non-empty string is `True`, whatever it says. That's why `DEBUG=false` needs comparing as text, not passing to `bool()`.
`bool()` accepts any value, so nothing is raised.
`bool()` always gives back `True` or `False`, never the string itself.

questions.q:
Predict the output:

```bash
echo "PORT=8000" > settings.env
echo "DEBUG=false" > settings.env
cat settings.env
```
explanations: The second `>` replaced the whole file, so the first line is gone.
Right. `>` replaces what's in the file each time. To add a line, use `>>`.
That would need `>>` on the second line, which adds to the end instead of replacing.
The second `echo` wrote its line, so the file isn't empty.

questions.q: You start PokeTeam and get "Address already in use" for port 8000. What's going on?
options: Another process is already listening on port 8000
PokeTeam's code has a syntax error
explanations: Ports on `localhost` don't need the internet at all.
Right. Only one program can listen on a port at a time. Often it's an old copy of your own server. `ss -ltnp` shows which one.
HTTPS normally uses 443. 8000 is a common development port.
A syntax error would stop Python before it tried to use the port at all.

questions.q:
Predict the output, in a fresh Ubuntu tab:

```bash
POKETEAM_MODE=dev
python3 -c 'import os; print(os.environ.get("POKETEAM_MODE", "unset"))'
```
explanations: That needs `export`. Without it, the variable stays in the shell and Python never gets a copy.
Right. `POKETEAM_MODE=dev` on its own line isn't exported, so Python's environment doesn't have it and `.get` falls back to `"unset"`.
`os.environ.get` gives back a value, never the name and value together.
`.get` with a default never raises a `KeyError`. Plain `os.environ["POKETEAM_MODE"]` would.

questions.q: What does `grep ERROR app.log | wc -l` print?
options: The lines of `app.log` that contain ERROR
How many lines of `app.log` contain ERROR
How many lines `app.log` has in total
explanations: `grep` keeps only the matching lines, and `wc -l` doesn't print lines at all.
That's what `grep ERROR app.log` alone prints. The pipe passes those lines on to `wc -l`.
Right. `grep` keeps the ERROR lines, and `wc -l` counts what it receives.
`wc -l` only counts what `grep` passed it, not the whole file.
